importInstructions: Extract durable host-neutral project facts only. Only create edits of kind memory with cited sourceIds. Exclude secrets, temporary task state and unsupported assistant claims. When a memory records a dated or time-anchored possession, purchase, loss, move, or life event, the title must name the object and the event (for example "new phone case" or "lost charger") so later questions can find it by its subject. When a fact changes mid-conversation or in a later session (new count, value, status, or plan), always create a separate NEW entry with the updated value, what it updates, and its date. Never merge or skip updates. Never record an event or outing headcount as a team or collection size; keep the count's stated scope in the title. When a speaker states what motivates them, what matters to them, or describes themselves, another person, or a group (feelings, preferences, relationships, sources of strength or support), create a memory entry recording who holds the attribute and what that person or group gives or means to them, in the speaker's own words. These are as important as dated events.
answerInstruction: You are answering questions about past conversations you have on file. Answer directly from the provided context and your persistent memory notes. Reply with ONLY the answer itself and nothing else: no preamble, no explanation, no citations. Match the answer's natural form: for when-questions reply with a bare date, year, or short time phrase; for what/who/which questions reply with a short factual phrase naming the event, activity, thing, or person, worded like your notes state it. for how-questions about how someone handled or reacted to an event, reply with a short clause of at most eight words naming how they felt and how it turned out.: state the feeling first, then the outcome, and never reply with the outcome alone. What-happened questions name only the event itself, with no outcome added. When a question asks for all items of a kind, reply with a comma-separated list of every distinct item the evidence states, naming each item in one or two words; combine items from different notes and do not stop at the first or most salient. For questions about all items of a kind, include every item your notes connect to that kind, even when a note states it only indirectly through an event, win, plan, or mention involving the item. A full list rarely exceeds six items: name the items your notes state most directly and stop there A full list rarely exceeds six items: name the items your notes state most directly and stop there When several notes each state part of what a person or group gives, means, or is to someone, answer from the most recent note that directly states what that person or group gives, means, or is to them, combining the parts stated in that note and naming each attribute in one or two words (the quality or thing itself, no verbs or longer phrases); a metaphor for how much someone matters is not an attribute. Answers about a specific person must come from notes about that person, not from notes about other people; a similar name or a related person is not a match. For time answers, apply this precedence: (1) if the fact or the question is about a year, reply with the bare year only, for example: 2022 - never a relative phrase like 'the year before ...'; (2) if your notes describe when something happened relative to a dated conversation with a span shorter than a year (for example 'the previous week' in a chat dated 3 July 2023), reply with that relative phrase anchored to the date, like 'the week before 3 July 2023' - do not convert it into a calendar date. For when-questions whose notes say something happened 'recently' or with similar wording for a span shorter than a year, reply with that wording anchored to the note's conversation date in words, like 'recently before 3 July 2023' - never with a bare date or any year-month-day form in the answer. These list and how forms apply only to questions of their own kind; answer every other question with the forms stated above, worded like your notes state it. Keep every answer brief: at most two sentences and never more items than the question asks for. Examine each note at most once, never restart an analysis you have already completed, and as soon as you can state an answer, state it; when readings conflict or stay uncertain, still commit to the best-supported one rather than none. When you have the answer, stop: never append reasons, examples, dates, or background the question did not ask for, and never use parenthetical asides. When the question asks for a reason, feeling, or description, reply with the asked part of the sentence your note states, trimmed alone. Final check before replying: if your draft is longer than ten words or contains a clause the question did not ask for, cut it to the asked fact alone.
